title: Electrically switchable one-dimensional quadrupolar excitons in lateral double heterojunctions
abstract: Two neighboring lateral interfaces provide a spatial degree of freedom for controlling one-dimensional charge-transfer excitons within a single semiconductor monolayer. We investigate a type-II WS2-MoS2-WS2 double heterojunction using an effective-mass two-particle Hamiltonian with a screened Coulomb interaction. For equivalent left and right interfaces at zero electric field,inter-interface coupling produces energetically split even- and odd-parity exciton states, each with zero permanent dipole. An electric field perpendicular to the interfaces continuously converts the lower state from a quadrupolar superposition with a quadratic Stark shift into a predominantly single-interface dipolar exciton with an approximately linear shift. The spatially resolved calculation gives binding energies of approximately 104 and 100 meV, a doublet splitting of 4.6 meV, and a crossover field of 0.87 V/um for a representative 1.5-nm MoS2 strip. Projection tests show that the lowest doublet controls the response near this crossover. Strip width tunes the coupling much more strongly than the binding energy, providing geometric control of the low-field Stark sensitivity. These results establish a continuum-model route to electrically reconfigurable one-dimensional quadrupolar excitons.
summary: This theoretical work examines how excitons confined in a double heterojunction can be electrically switched between a quadrupolar and a dipolar state. By solving the effective-mass Hamiltonian, the authors predict a clear crossover in the exciton's optical response as an external electric field is applied. This demonstrates a novel, geometrically controllable mechanism for manipulating quantum excitonic states in 2D materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the electrical control and switching of one-dimensional quadrupolar exciton states within semiconductor double heterojunctions.
main_result: Applying a perpendicular electric field can continuously switch the exciton state from a quadrupolar superposition (zero permanent dipole) to a dipolar state (linear Stark shift).
method: The research employs an effective-mass two-particle Hamiltonian solved via basis expansion and numerical diagonalization techniques.
model_or_system: The system is a type-II WS2-MoS2-WS2 double heterojunction, modeled using an effective-mass Hamiltonian incorporating screened Coulomb interactions.
key_observables: Binding energies ($\approx 100$ meV), doublet splitting ($\approx 4.6$ meV), crossover field ($\approx 0.87 	ext{ V}/\mu	ext{m}$), and the electric quadrupole moment.
important_parameters: Strip width ($L$), applied electric field ($F$), and the material band offsets ($\Delta E_c, \Delta E_v$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes constant scalar masses and uses a phenomenological screening parameter for the Coulomb interaction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system structure, potential profiles, and the evolution of exciton states from quadrupolar to dipolar character under an electric field. Tables quantify binding energies, splitting, and sensitivity to structural parameters.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the zero-field coupling leading to even/odd parity states, then models the field-induced transition from the quadrupolar to the dipolar regime, concluding with quantitative measurements of energy shifts and geometric tunability.
why_interesting: The concept of electrically reconfigurable excitons, particularly the transition between symmetry-protected quadrupolar and dipole states, provides a platform for understanding tunable quantum optical responses in solid-state nanostructures.
